stories.teaser: More than 100,000 coats donated to Israelis in need
stories.headline: “Hug for Winter” returns: an Israeli coat drive that has collected more than 100,000 coats for people in need
stories.why: About 12,500 coats last year, collected at hundreds of points across Israel.
texts:
Open your closet, and your heart.

Israel’s “Hug for Winter” coat drive is back. Since it began, it has collected more than 100,000 coats for people and families in need, about 12,500 last year alone.

“The power of ‘Hug for Winter’ is the ability of an entire community to rally around a simple act,” says Ido Lotan of Ruach Tova.

#Israel #Winter #Volunteering #SocialImpact

More than 100,000 coats, and counting.

“Hug for Winter,” run by Ruach Tova with Social Transport, Project Yosef and Pitchon Lev, collects clean, good-condition coats at hundreds of points across Israel, run by local authorities, private homes and businesses. Last year it gathered about 12,500 coats for people who needed them.

#Israel #Winter #Volunteering #SocialImpact

What if your old coat could keep someone else warm this winter?

That’s how “Hug for Winter” works: people drop off coats they no longer use at hundreds of collection points, and partner organizations pass them on, respectfully, to people and families in need. More than 100,000 coats so far.

An idea any community could borrow.

#Israel #Winter #Volunteering #SocialImpact

stories.teaser: Common drugs put a third of mice with ‘Type 1.5 diabetes’ into remission
stories.headline: Bar-Ilan researchers use three common drugs to put a third of mice with “Type 1.5 diabetes” into remission
stories.why: Published in MedComm; blood biomarkers predicted which mice would respond. Human trials are still needed.
texts:
Hope for an often-missed kind of diabetes.

Bar-Ilan University researchers led by Dr. Ron Piran gave mice with LADA, sometimes called “Type 1.5 diabetes,” a combination of three existing drugs. About a third went into complete remission, no longer needing insulin, and grew new insulin-producing cells. The work is in mice; human trials would come next.

#Israel #BarIlan #Diabetes #Health

About 30% of treated mice: diabetes-free for weeks after treatment ended.

Bar-Ilan’s team combined GABA, the diabetes drug sitagliptin and the acid-reflux drug omeprazole. Two blood biomarkers, Adgrb1 and Chd5, predicted in advance which mice would respond. Published in MedComm, the study points toward personalized care, though it has not yet been tested in people.

#Israel #BarIlan #Diabetes #Health

Could already-approved drugs help people with “Type 1.5 diabetes”?

In mice, a Bar-Ilan University study found a three-drug combination put about a third into remission.

“We don’t need to prove their safety, and people already take them,” says Dr. Ron Piran. The next step would be a human clinical trial.

#Israel #BarIlan #Diabetes #Health
stories.og_title: Israeli scientists use common drugs to cure 30% of mice with 'Type 1.5 diabetes'

stories.teaser: Two gorilla sisters built a “living ladder” to reach a branch
stories.headline: Tel Aviv University researchers document two gorillas at Ramat Gan Safari building a “living ladder” together
stories.why: Published in Primates; three untrained cooperation events recorded in 2021, 2024 and 2025.
texts:
Teamwork, gorilla style.

At Ramat Gan Safari, half-sisters Amelia and Lisha, two western lowland gorillas, worked together to reach a branch: Lisha stood on all fours as a platform and Amelia climbed onto her back. Tel Aviv University researchers documented it three times, in 2021, 2024 and 2025. Neither had been trained. Published in Primates.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Gorillas #Nature

Three times, same roles, no training.

Tel Aviv University researchers Michael Levitsky and Prof. Israel Hershkovitz documented two gorillas at Ramat Gan Safari forming a “living ladder.” In September 2024, one stood on the other’s back to break off a branch about 4.5 meters up. The study was published in the journal Primates.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Gorillas #Nature

“Sometimes, our surprise tells us more about our expectations of animals than their actual abilities,” says Samocha, head of the primate section at Ramat Gan Safari.

Two gorilla sisters there were filmed cooperating to reach high branches, one acting as a step for the other. Tel Aviv University researchers say it may offer clues to how early humans cooperated.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Gorillas #Nature
stories.og_title: Two Gorillas, One Goal: A Remarkable Display of Teamwork

stories.teaser: Hebrew University scientists unlock how petunias control scent and survive heat
stories.headline: Hebrew University scientists find the “brake” on flower scent, and make petunias more heat-resistant
stories.why: Published in Plant Physiology; the findings could help breed heat-tolerant peppers, tomatoes and eggplants.
texts:
Cracking the language of flowers.

At the Hebrew University’s Faculty of Agriculture in Rehovot, Dr. Oded Skliter and Prof. Alexander Vainstein found a protein mechanism that acts as a brake on petunia scent. Using gene editing to release it, flowers produced much more of their vanilla-like and clove-like scent compounds. Published in Plant Physiology.

#Israel #HebrewUniversity #Agriculture #Science

Bigger scent, better heat tolerance.

Hebrew University researchers disabled a protein that holds back scent production in petunias. The gene-edited flowers released far more fragrance, and under extreme heat they shrank less than ordinary ones. The team says this could help breed heat-resistant peppers, tomatoes and eggplants, which belong to the same plant family.

#Israel #HebrewUniversity #Agriculture #Science

“We were able to understand how the flower connects color and scent, and found a way to help it cope with extreme weather,” says Prof. Alexander Vainstein of the Hebrew University.

The study, published in Plant Physiology, shows how basic plant science could lead to new vegetable varieties for a hotter climate.

#Israel #HebrewUniversity #Agriculture #Science

stories.teaser: A sinus scope that bends, and an ear scope that frees a surgeon’s hand
stories.headline: Two Israeli engineer brothers built surgeons a camera that sees around corners
stories.why: Founded by brothers Ehud and Eran Bendory; both scopes are FDA-cleared and used at US hospitals including Cincinnati Children’s.
texts:
Two Israeli brothers, both engineers, built surgeons a camera that sees around corners.

Ehud and Eran Bendory founded 3NT Medical in 2013 and started by asking ENT surgeons what was missing. The answer: standard sinus scopes are stiff rods that look straight ahead. Their Peregrine scope has a tip that bends, with views from 0° to 140°. In an early test it showed almost all sinus landmarks, versus about 40–50% with a standard scope.

#Israel #MedTech #Innovation #Surgery

Ear surgeons often work one-handed, because the other hand holds the camera.

Israeli company 3NT Medical, founded by brothers Ehud and Eran Bendory, built the Colibri, a slim ear scope with suction built in, so surgeons can operate with both hands. It’s FDA-cleared, and at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital the director of pediatric otolaryngology calls it “an integral tool in our pediatric otology surgeries.”

#Israel #MedTech #ChildrensHealth #Surgery

They weren’t doctors. They were engineers who listened.

Brothers Ehud and Eran Bendory asked ENT surgeons what their tools couldn’t do, then built it: a sinus scope whose tip bends to see around corners, and an ear scope with built-in suction that frees a surgeon’s second hand. Their company, 3NT Medical, has both scopes FDA-cleared and in use at hospitals in the US.

#Israel #MedTech #Innovation #Engineering
stories.og_title: Two Israeli Brothers Built Surgeons a Camera That Sees Around Corners

stories.teaser: Dozens of older women do paid work four hours a day
stories.headline: In Sderot, a work club gives seniors purpose, company and a paycheck
stories.why: Run by the Ra’ut association with JDC Israel and the city; members split all client payments equally, and the club keeps nothing.
texts:
“We are not elderly. I don’t like that word. We are mature people.”

That’s Yoki Solimani-Daniali, 76, one of dozens of seniors, almost all women, who come four hours a day to a work club in Sderot run by the Ra’ut association with the city’s welfare department and JDC Israel. They pack fragrances, candles and gift boxes for businesses, and get paid for it.

#Israel #SocialImpact #Aging #Community

“It’s like a family to me, and it gives me a lot of energy,” says Ludmila Dubkov, 78.

She’s a member of a work club for older adults in Sderot, run by the Ra’ut association with JDC Israel and the city’s welfare department. Members come four hours a day to do real, paid work for businesses. Einav Avraham has managed the club for the past 12 years.

#Israel #SocialImpact #Aging #Community

How do you give retirees purpose, company and a paycheck?

In Sderot, a work club run by the Ra’ut association with JDC Israel takes on real jobs from businesses: packing fragrances, candles and holiday gift boxes. At the end of each month the club bills each client and splits the total equally among members, about 800–1,000 shekels each. The club keeps nothing.

An idea any community could borrow.

#Israel #SocialImpact #Aging #Community
